But while you can have some/most of the benefits Zig has from modern C, I think an underrated benefit is the language culture. As a different language it was the opportunity for a reset, e.g. it's idiomatic Zig to pass allocators to functions, meaning every library in Zig will work this way. You could do that in C, but none or very few libraries do that so whenever you reach out to third-party dependencies (which is not a lot, in C as in Zig) you have to fight against C's traditional patterns.

Some PHP functions (e.g. opening a file) return a `resource` type, but PHP has no official way to declare it. So the right way is to declare `mixed` as an official type (which means `any`) and fix that declaration with a phpdoc comment. Phpdoc provides generics (named "templates", à la C++), e.g. `iterable<Something>` where `iterable` is an official PHP type (which is awfully imprecise without phpdoc). Phpdoc has tuples and (associative) array shapes, e.g. `@return list{int, \Error}`. In past PHP versions, the type system was worse because the internal types were ambiguous: types were implicitly nullable, i.e. `string` meant `null|string`. When PHP gradually added sum types, they fixed that ambiguity.

> so tell me what benefits that has over having no dmarc record at all ? The the existence of a DMARC assertion record in the DNS changes how the MTA (the receiving system) assesses the authentication of the message and  authorization of the sender with SPF and/or DKIM, as per rfc7489 (and now also rfc9989). No DMARC results in the MTA falling back to the original assessment method as defined in the original SPF and DKIM RFCs. These RFCs have design flaws and don't define the assessment flow all that well, they leave a lot up to the MTA's digression/interpretation. So, the existence of a DMARC record with p=none is fundamentally different over not publishing a DMARC assertion record at all. It's just that with p=none you don't enforce the MTA to reject the email if it fails authentication/authorization, you're leaving it up to the MTAs digression.

To have LESS friction you need MORE signals, ones that add up to "this action is low risk, proceed" as a cumulative risk score. Kind of like credit card transactions... most transactions go through silently because the issuer scores them on merchant, amount, device and history, and you only get the step-up prompt when the score is off. "Manual Approval" and "Bypass Everything" are both what you ship when you have no signals.

It depends. With conventional AWD (like all Subarus), you are correct that there is significant energy loss due to the AWD because there is a drivetrain to the rear wheels, even if it is not delivering power.
Many hybrids, however, have AWD and they work by having a second, small electric motor that powers the rear wheels only when needed. That means no physical drivetrain to the rear wheels, so no energy loss. That's why a hybrid Toyota RAV4 AWD gets about 15% better gas mileage than the smaller and lighter hybrid Subaru Crosstrek AWD.
The disadvantage of the electric motor approach is that it cannot deliver as much power to the rear wheels as a conventional physical AWD drivetrain can. That said, probably only an issue in deep mud or snow.

The problem with a sudden collapse of birthrates in most of the industrialised world is the instability it will cause. This causes a massive pressure for mass migrations from very different cultures, as well as strong generational imbalances. Ideally most of the world would gravitate towards stable 2.1 replacement rates, or not too far from it. IMO 1.9 or even 1.7 wouldn't be something to worry too much about (many economists would disagree). But going even below there, and adjusting very fast is worrisome. It guarantees a socioeconomic shock.

A much better faraday cage is matroiska doll nesting of  two  different size trash cans with a non-conductive platform supporting inside smaller can. The air gap and double conducting surfaces really help. And with the different circumference of the smaller can's rim there'll be a different resonant freq that gets let in. So while the outside seam may pass ~339 MHz without any attenuation the inner seam might pass ~450 MHz and so both unintentional passbands will get at least the minimum ~20dB attenuation per can.

For purchases, the US has debit cards and Zelle. Banks instantly exchange non-revocable promises to pay and the money follows at the end of the day. This is more capital (cash) efficient because it allows netting. One key here is that everybody in the US banking system is under the same regulators (Federal Reserve, FDIC/NCUA) so there's greater trust that they won't go under before the cash comes. A very important point is that debit cards offer consumer protections (chargebacks for unsatisfactory goods). FedNow, Zelle, wires, ACH do not and people have lost money by scams this way. If you don't need it right that second, same-day ACH is widely used, and again the delay allows more efficient netting. The Clearing House's CHIPS is a good in-between, it's not guaranteed instant, but uses an algorithm to match transactions as fast as possible with constrained float.
